h1: The 8 Best Small Raised Garden Beds for Patios and Backyards, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Small Raised Garden Beds: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 small galvanized raised garden beds compared on footprint, 12 inch depth, soil volume and multi-bed kit value.
summary: The Meberam 2-pack of 6x3x1 foot galvanized beds is the small raised garden bed set to buy for most yards, giving you 36 cubic feet of growing space for a low price. The Bujijun 2-pack is a near twin, FOYUEE sells the same size at a higher bucket, and the Utopia Home 4x2x1 is the pick when a patio corner is all you have.
intro: The common mistake with a small raised bed is shopping for the footprint and forgetting the depth. A 12 inch wall is enough for lettuce, herbs, radishes and bush beans, but it is the minimum for tomatoes and peppers, and it leaves nothing for deep carrots or potatoes. The ground under the bed matters too, since a shallow box leans on the native soil below it.

So we ranked these by how much real planting volume you get for the money. We reviewed eight galvanized steel beds from their listings, comparing footprint, the 12 inch height, pack count, price bucket and how much detail each seller gives. These listings share the same core material, so differences come down to size, multi-bed value and how well the page documents what you are buying.

products.name: Meberam 2 Pack 6x3x1FT Galvanized Raised Garden Beds Kit Outdoor
products.verdict: Two 6x3x1 foot galvanized beds in one box, for $25 to $50.
products.description:
The Meberam kit includes two galvanized steel beds, each 6 feet long, 3 feet wide and 12 inches tall. That works out to 18 cubic feet of soil per bed and 36 across the pair, and the whole set falls in the $25 to $50 bucket.

It takes first place because per-bed cost drops sharply when you buy two, and the 6x3 shape is the most useful small size: wide enough to plant three rows, narrow enough to reach the middle from either side without stepping in. Against the single-bed Tegarbed, you get double the growing area for a similar price.

Buy it if you want to start a small vegetable garden with two beds side by side. The caveat is that 12 inches limits deep-rooted crops, and the listing gives few details on assembly hardware.
pros: Two beds for a low price
6x3 size is easy to reach across
products.idealFor: First-time gardeners starting a two-bed vegetable plot.
products.skipIf: You want to grow deep-rooted crops.

products.name: Tegarbed 10x2x1FT Galvanized Raised Garden Bed
products.verdict: A 10 foot long, 2 foot wide bed for fence lines and narrow strips.
products.description:
The Tegarbed 10x2x1 is a single galvanized bed measuring 10 feet long, 2 feet wide and 12 inches tall. That gives 20 cubic feet of soil in a shape that fits a fence line or the edge of a patio. It sits in the $25 to $50 bucket.

It ranks fourth because the long, narrow format suits a different job than the 6x3 pairs: a row of herbs, lettuces or flowers along a wall. The 2 foot width means you can reach the whole bed from one side, which is handy against a fence. The tradeoff is that a 10 foot bed has long sides that can bow outward under the weight of wet soil without cross-bracing, and the listing does not say whether any is included.

Buy it if you have a long, narrow strip. Skip it if you want a square plot.

cons: Long walls may bow when full

whatMatters.detail: Multiply length, width and height in feet to get soil volume. A 6x3x1 bed holds 18 cubic feet and a 4x2x1 holds 8. Use this number to compare beds and to order soil, since bagged soil is sold by cubic foot.

Twelve inches suits lettuce, herbs, radishes, beans and most flowers. Tomatoes, peppers and carrots grow better with more depth, often 15 to 18 inches of loose soil, which can include the ground beneath if the bed has no bottom. Check the stated height on the listing.

Zinc-coated steel resists rot and does not host termites the way wood can. It can heat up in summer sun, so plant heat-sensitive crops away from the edges. Look for galvanized or similar coating in the title.
A bed 3 feet wide lets you reach the middle from either side. A 2 foot bed can sit against a fence and be reached from one side. Avoid beds wider than 4 feet.
Cut steel edges can be sharp, so wear gloves. Look for rolled or capped edges on the listing. Long beds may need cross-braces to hold their shape when filled.

faq.q: Do I need to line the bottom of a galvanized raised bed?
faq.a: Most are open-bottomed so roots reach the soil below. Lay cardboard or landscape fabric on the ground first to suppress weeds. Place the bed on level ground.

faq.q: What mistake do beginners make with raised beds?
faq.a: Buying too shallow and filling with poor soil. Use a mix of compost and topsoil, and plant deep-rooted crops only if the bed is deep enough. A level base also matters.

faq.q: Is a metal raised bed worth it over wood?
faq.a: Metal does not rot or attract termites, and lasts many seasons. It can heat up in summer, so mulch the soil and water more. Wood is cheaper but can decay.

faq.q: How do I assemble these beds?
faq.a: Lay out the panels, join them with the supplied hardware and tighten gradually. Wear gloves because steel edges can be sharp. Work on flat ground with a helper for long beds.

faq.q: How much soil do I need?
faq.a: Multiply length by width by height in feet. A 6x3x1 bed needs about 18 cubic feet, and a 4x2x1 about 8. Order a little extra, since soil settles after watering.

faq.q: Will galvanized steel harm my vegetables?
faq.a: Galvanized steel is widely used for gardening and the zinc coating is stable in normal soil. Very acidic soil can wear the coating faster. Check the manufacturer guidance on soil pH.

finalTake: The Meberam 2 Pack of 6x3x1 foot galvanized beds is the best small raised garden bed buy for most yards. Choose the Tegarbed 10x2x1 for a fence line and the Utopia Home 4x2x1 for a patio or balcony. Be cautious with the unsized single beds, since you cannot plan a garden without dimensions.
